title: FPRAS for #BIS
formal: Does \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\), counting all independent sets in an arbitrary finite simple bipartite graph, admit a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme? Precisely, do there exist one probabilistic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,k\geq1\) such that, for every encoded bipartite graph \(G\) and rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), the machine outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) within \(C(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)^k\) steps on every random tape and satisfies \[\Pr\big[(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)\leq\widehat Z\leq(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)\big]\geq\tfrac34?\] Here \(Z(G)\) is the number of independent vertex subsets, \(L\) is the complete encoded input length, and the probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair coin bits.
definitions: For an integer \(n\geq0\), the vertex set is \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), partitioned into disjoint specified sets \(U,V\), either of which may be empty. An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices with one endpoint in each part; there are no loops or parallel edges. An independent set is a subset \(I\subseteq U\cup V\) that contains no complete edge, and \(Z(G)=|\{I\subseteq U\cup V:I\text{ is independent}\}|\). Every independent set is counted once, with weight one, irrespective of its size or the number of its vertices in either part. The empty set is included, so \(Z(G)\geq1\), and the graph with no vertices has \(Z(G)=1\). Graphs may be disconnected and have isolated vertices, arbitrary degrees and parts of unequal sizes. Fix the following explicit finite-alphabet encoding. Write bin(j) for the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer j, with no leading zeros except in bin(0). An input is the string bin(n)#b#a#bin(r)#bin(s), where b has exactly n bits specifying part membership, a has exactly n(n−1)/2 bits specifying adjacency for pairs (i,j), i<j, in increasing lexicographic order, and integers r,s satisfy 0<r<s. Every adjacency bit equal to one must join vertices whose membership bits differ. The accuracy is \(\varepsilon=r/s\); the fraction need not be reduced. Thus isolated vertices are represented explicitly, and L counts all bits and separators, including both accuracy integers. The ceiling \(\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\) is taken after real division. An output encodes \(\widehat Z=p/q\) as bin(p)#bin(q), with integers \(p\geq0\), \(q\geq1\). The machine has finite control and finitely many ordinary work tapes, with a stream of independent unbiased random bits. All input reading, bit computation, random-bit access and output writing are charged as Turing-machine steps; exact arithmetic on unbounded integers or reals is not a unit-cost operation. There is no oracle, advice, quantum resource or random input-graph assumption. The same program and constants C,k must work for all graph sizes, degrees, bipartitions and accuracies. Malformed strings are rejected by returning 0/1 within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps on every random tape, after increasing the common constants if needed. Deterministic algorithms are permitted as the special case that ignores the random bits.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that a single algorithm and constants C,k meet the stated worst-case bit-cost bound, rational-output requirement and per-instance relative-error guarantee, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. The negative direction must rule out every uniform fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme. Equivalently, every candidate satisfying the polynomial runtime and output conditions must have some valid input \((G,\varepsilon)\) on which its probability of a correct relative approximation is strictly less than \(3/4\). Showing a failure of a particular sampler, a finite running-time lower bound, or difficulty of exact counting does not establish this universal impossibility. A conditional lower bound, for example one assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), is not an unconditional negative resolution unless the assumed separation is also proved. The positive direction must cover every input graph and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), with a polynomial degree independent of those inputs; expected runtime alone does not match the specified bound without a proof yielding the required always-bounded scheme. The target is existence of an approximation algorithm with its requested accuracy parameter, so a fixed numerical tolerance of 1/100 does not replace the quantified relative-error requirement. A deterministic fully polynomial scheme would meet the target, but is not required.
why: The canonical unresolved boundary in approximate counting: many counting problems share its approximation difficulty, while exact counting hardness does not settle whether a randomized relative approximation is efficient. A general scheme would transfer to problems reducible to it with preserved approximation guarantees; an impossibility proof would separate this central family from the counting problems with known fully polynomial schemes.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved boundary in approximate counting, with broad approximation-preserving consequences and a well-defined gap between FPRAS and hardness evidence.

progress.text: Curticapean, Dell, Fomin, Goldberg and Lapinskas publish the fixed-parameter perspective, distinguishing total bipartite counting from fixed-size restrictions and recording its conjecturally intermediate approximation status.
Liao–Lin–Lu–Mao prove an FPTAS for almost every fixed-\(\Delta\)-regular bipartite graph when \(\Delta\geq53\); the randomness in this statement concerns the input graph, not an all-input guarantee.

Carlson–Davies–Kolla–Potukuchi publish the fixed-density regular-graph FPRAS at ICALP. The linked 2023 preprint has a different title; the conference title, author list, date and exact \(d=\lfloor\delta|V(G)|/2\rfloor\) hypothesis have been reconciled.

Narang–Perkins–Wang–Wee post hardness claims for balanced and fixed-slice counts while explicitly retaining the ordinary unrestricted #BIS question as open. This remains the only listed version as checked on 14 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: An independent set need not be maximal or maximum. For an edgeless graph on \(n\) vertices the count is \(2^n\), whereas a complete bipartite graph with part sizes \(a,b\) has \(2^a+2^b-1\) independent sets: any subset of either part is allowed, with the empty set counted only once. In every bipartite graph all subsets of each part are independent, so the count can be exponentially large even though the instance and the binary representation of its count have polynomial length. The requested error is relative to that count, not to the number of vertices.

Exact counting and approximate counting have different known boundaries. The 2019 primary source recalls that exact \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\) is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete even at maximum degree three, while efficient relative approximation is known when all degrees on one side are at most five. It also recalls that allowing maximum degree six already recovers the full approximation difficulty. Here \(\#\mathrm P\) consists of counts of accepting computation paths of nondeterministic polynomial-time machines; hardness of computing such counts exactly does not itself rule out an FPRAS.

Approximation-preserving reductions allow a counting problem to be solved using relative approximations for another, with polynomial overhead and polynomially controlled requested precision. The literature contains many problems equivalent to \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\) under such reductions, including problems about constrained assignments and statistical-mechanics models. The 2019 authors describe the family as conjecturally intermediate: neither an FPRAS nor NP-hardness of approximation is known for the unrestricted target. This is a description of the open complexity landscape, not a proved impossibility theorem.

The hard-core partition function is \(Z_G(\lambda)=\sum_{I\text{ independent}}\lambda^{|I|}\), for a positive parameter \(\lambda\) called fugacity. It normalizes the probability distribution assigning each independent set probability \(\lambda^{|I|}/Z_G(\lambda)\). The card fixes \(\lambda=1\), so every independent set has equal weight. Results for other fugacities or for distributions conditioned on a prescribed set size must be checked against this unweighted total count.

Liao, Lin, Lu and Mao give an FPTAS for almost every \(\Delta\)-regular bipartite graph when the fixed degree \(\Delta\geq53\), including the unweighted count. Regular means that every vertex has the same degree. Their probability is over a uniformly chosen graph with \(n\) vertices on each side, and tends to one as \(n\to\infty\); the approximation algorithm itself is deterministic. This is a substantial result for typical inputs, but it does not guarantee success on every bipartite graph as required here.

The ICALP 2024 dense-graph theorem gives an FPRAS for every fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\) on graphs with \(2n\) vertices that are \(\lfloor\delta n\rfloor\)-regular. Its constants and polynomial running-time degree may depend on the fixed density \(\delta\). Consequently, allowing \(\delta\) to decrease with the input size does not turn the stated theorem into a fully polynomial bound for all bipartite graphs. The paper’s exponential-form relative error and the card’s \(1\pm\varepsilon\) convention are equivalent for the existence of an FPRAS after a constant-factor change in the accuracy parameter.

The August 2026 preprint studies a different count: only independent sets occupying the two sides equally, or prescribed numbers of vertices on the two sides. Theorem 1.2 reports an approximation hardness threshold for the balanced partition function. In particular, at fugacity one and maximum degree six, it reports no FPRAS unless \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{RP}\). Here NP is nondeterministic polynomial time, and RP is randomized polynomial-time decision with no false positives and acceptance probability at least one half on positive instances. The balance restriction changes which sets are counted, so this conditional result does not establish hardness of the unrestricted total count on this card. The new proof has not been independently verified in this review.

The same August preprint explicitly states that ordinary \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\) is neither known to admit an FPRAS nor known to be NP-hard to approximate. A slow-mixing Markov chain is likewise an obstruction to that chain, rather than to all possible randomized approximation algorithms. The remaining question concerns the existence of any uniform scheme satisfying the full worst-case guarantee.

sentences: The #BIS problem counts all independent vertex subsets of an arbitrary finite simple bipartite graph, including the empty set.

The question asks for one uniform randomized bit algorithm with polynomial runtime in the complete input length and inverse requested relative accuracy, succeeding with probability at least three quarters on every instance.
Acceptance requires a full Lean-checked construction with an every-random-tape runtime bound, or a proof excluding every such scheme without an unresolved extra assumption.
The problem represents a central approximation class whose apparent intermediate complexity is not settled by hardness of exact counting.
The checked2026 literature still leaves the total count open, while typical regular inputs, dense regular graphs and balanced or fixed-size counts have distinct known results.
